claims.text: The starting powder mixture is equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting powder has no pre-existing lattice strain or nanocrystalline structure.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling generates a critical level of lattice strain in CoCrFeNiTi.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling refines CoCrFeNiTi to a nanocrystalline grain size.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the activation-energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
Milling raises the internal energy of the FCC phase and thereby effectively lowers the VEC threshold for the FCC-to-BCC transition.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the stability of the FCC/BCC phases in this CoCrFeNiTi transition.
SPS at 1000°C provides sufficient diffusion to densify the milled alloy rapidly.
The proposed milling and SPS treatment will produce a relative density greater than 98%.
SPS at 1000°C will avoid significant nucleation of Ti-rich HCP precipitates.
The processed alloy will retain a dominant BCC or mixed BCC+FCC metastable solid solution stabilized by strain.
The processed alloy will have significantly greater Vickers hardness than a conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
The predicted hardness increase arises from Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening and strain hardening.
Conventionally arc-melted and cast CoCrFeNiTi has a coarse dendritic microstructure, Ti-rich segregation, low hardness, and residual porosity.
A sintering temperature of 1050°C is the upper threshold for avoiding Ti diffusion sufficient to trigger HCP precipitation.
Sintering above 1050°C triggers rapid grain growth that degrades mechanical properties.
Low-load Vickers testing at 10 g or 25 g minimizes indentation-size effects.
Low-load Vickers testing can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
At 1000°C, HCP content should remain at or below 5 vol% and grain size should remain at or below 500 nm.
An 1100°C SPS sample is predicted to lose hardness through excessive grain growth or phase decomposition relative to the 1000°C sample.

contradictions.description: The boundary predicts that 1100°C should cause excessive grain growth or phase decomposition and therefore lower hardness relative to 1000°C, but the falsification rule incorrectly states that observing this predicted lower hardness would falsify the boundary effect rather than support it.
